title: Marrons glacés
subtitle: French candied chestnuts in vanilla syrup
excerpt: Marrons glacés are whole chestnuts slowly impregnated with vanilla-scented sugar syrup over several days, then glazed to a crystalline finish. They are a French luxury confection associated with Ardèche, eaten at Christmas and given as gifts. The technique takes four to five days of repeated syrup soaks, not hours of labour, but time, and produces chestnuts that are tender, intensely sweet, and perfumed with vanilla.
sourceNotes: Marrons glacés are considered one of France's most prestigious confections, with production centred on the Ardèche region, which grows the majority of French chestnuts. The modern commercial method was developed in the 19th century, though the technique of preserving chestnuts in sugar syrup appears in French cookery from at least the 17th century. Commercial producers use vacuum impregnation to speed up the process; home versions replicate the traditional slow soak method, where the syrup concentration is gradually increased over multiple days until the chestnut interior is fully saturated. A true marron glacé uses the inner nut of a grafted chestnut variety (marron de Lyon or similar) with a single lobe; ordinary chestnuts from the hedge may split.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze individually wrapped in parchment in an airtight container. Defrost at room temperature for 2 hours.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Begin 5 days before you want to serve them; the process cannot be rushed.

content.text: Marrons glacés take five days to make. The chestnuts are boiled and peeled on day one, then soaked in progressively stronger sugar syrup on each of the following days, and glazed on the last. None of the daily steps takes more than 30 minutes of active time; most of the process is resting. The result is a whole chestnut that is deeply sweet, perfumed with vanilla, and tender all the way through.

items.prepNote: plus 200 g more for each subsequent syrup

content.text: Score a cross through the flat side of each chestnut. Boil in water for 5 minutes, then, working in small batches, keeping the others in the hot water, peel off both the outer shell and the thin inner skin while they're hot. The skin comes away easily while warm and becomes very difficult once cold. Discard any that crumble or are too small to peel intact. Place the peeled chestnuts in a wide saucepan.

Make a syrup from 600 g sugar, 600 ml water, and the vanilla pods. Bring to the boil, stir to dissolve, and pour over the peeled chestnuts in the pan. The syrup should cover them. Bring back to a bare simmer for 1 minute, then remove from the heat. Cover and leave to soak overnight at room temperature.
Days 2 to 4, building the syrup concentration

Each day, drain the syrup into a saucepan, add 100 g more granulated sugar, and dissolve over heat. Bring to the boil, pour back over the chestnuts, simmer for 1 minute, then cover and leave overnight. The syrup becomes progressively more viscous. By day 4 it will coat the back of a spoon thickly. Handle the chestnuts as little as possible; they become more fragile as they absorb syrup.

Drain the chestnuts and lift each one carefully onto a wire rack set over a tray. Make a thin glaze syrup from 200 g sugar and 100 ml water, cooked to 113°C. Using a skewer or two forks, dip each chestnut briefly in the glaze and return to the rack. Leave to dry in a warm oven at 80°C for 1 hour, or at room temperature for several hours, until the surface is dry and crystalline. Wrap individually in parchment or cellophane. They keep in a cool place for up to 2 weeks.
